The question of whether children learn language skills from television is contested across the retrieved evidence. Well-designed educational programs like Sesame Street have been shown to improve cognitive, literacy, and social outcomes for children aged 3–5, and educational TV can teach complex reading skills including informational text comprehension [d2, d4]; watching TV with same-language subtitles also improves decoding, vocabulary, and comprehension skills [d8]. However, multiple studies find no benefit or even harm: toddlers who watched the Baby Wordsworth educational DVD for six weeks showed no language gains compared to non-viewers [d11], children playing with blocks independently developed better language and cognitive skills than peers watching Baby Einstein videos [d10], and a UCLA study of 275 families found that TV viewing had no effect on language development (neither positive nor negative), while back-and-forth conversation contributed most to future language scores [d12]. A meta-analysis notes that screen time can displace critical caregiver-child interactions and create a "transfer deficit," though educational programs may still offer some benefit [d7], and one review explicitly acknowledges that "there is still controversy from several existing studies on the relationship between television exposure and language development" [d6]. Overall, the evidence suggests that any language benefits from television are conditional on program quality, child age, and adult co-viewing, and that real-time social interaction consistently outperforms screen-based learning [d1, d10].
